title: Precepts and the Path
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: In this Soto Zen dharma talk, the teacher reflects on the importance of cultivating peace and presence in the face of uncertainty, using the example of Tony Long's embodiment of "peaceful way" despite his physical illness. They share a koan about Jin Yuan, who lets go of attachment to labels like "life" or "death," finding freedom in the present moment. This teaching invites listeners to consider what it means to be fully present and at peace, even when faced with challenges or uncertainty.

sentences.text: So welcome to our Sunday Zen and Life program.
A week ago, we were all sitting together in separate places.
Desiree was at Tassajara, we were at Samish Island.
I have a little bit of a hard time coming back this year; my house hasn't really recovered from the mess yet.
I'm working on it; it's a work in progress like everything else.
So I know that our big theme this year is the Eightfold Path.
I'm going to take half a step off it.
I am happy to see you, and I hope that you're having a great summer.
It's warm outside; the ice cream truck jingles by the house every once in a while.
When it's cool, all the windows and doors are open.
It looks like I'll have a bumper crop of apples and a few Asian pears too.
I'm so grateful to share this day of plenty; I am so grateful to be alive.
Today, I won't start out with a poem, but with a brief quote from Gensho Koan.
*As all things are Buddha Dharma, there is delusion and realization, practice, birth and death.
And there are Buddhas and sentient beings.
As the myriad things are without an abiding self, there is no delusion, no realization, no Buddha, no sentient being, no birth and death.
The Buddha way is basically leaping clear of the many and the one.
Thus, there are birth and death, delusion and realization, sentient beings and Buddhas, yet in attachment blossoms fall, and in aversion wheat spread.
Delusion and realization, sentient beings and Buddhas, yet in attachment blossoms fall, and in aversion wheat spread.
Yet in attachment blossoms fall, and in aversion wheat spread.
Loss and gain, come and go in this landscape of continuous change.
And I would like to tell you a little bit about loss and gain.
And a remarkable person and Dharma friend, Kanon Hedo, completely rooted, peaceful way, Tony Long.*
Tony signed up for the precepts class in 2022, which was obviously on Zoom.
I was one of the teachers, and I locked on early to greet everyone as they were showing up.
Tony was the first.
He kind of said, "Hi, my name is Tony.
I'm here because I'm dying.
I don't have long to live.
And I want to study the precepts in preparation for my death."
Well, what an introduction.
Tony really participated fully in a very engaged way in the class.
The members of his small study group really cherished and loved him.
He contributed so much, not only to his small study group, but to all of us who participated.
Tony didn't ask for it, but it was very obvious that he was taking the precepts study very seriously, and he could have come and joined our Sangha for Choklai ceremony.
However, he was too sick to travel, and it was very exhausting for him.
So Hannah Sullivan and I traveled to Yakima to Choklai for Tony.
It was so heartwarming that when we brought up the Zoom screen for his Choklai to connect him to Red Cedar, there were so many members from the Red Cedar Sangha there.
It was just wonderful, and he was really taken aback a little bit by that.
We did the ceremony, and it was very moving and it was deeply felt.
Afterwards, Tony and his amazing wife Rosemary told us stories from their life, how they met and courted or not courted.
Tony told us of his many years as a teacher and as someone who is helping youth, his efforts to help people.
Both Tony and Rosemary were like one unit; they were the most amazing couple I've ever met in my life.
They showed their big hearts, and maybe it's time for a poem after all.
*Peaceful Life by Dainin Katagiri Voshi: Being told that it is impossible one believes in despair.
Is that so?
Being told that it is possible one believes in excitement.
That's right.
But whichever is chosen, it does not fit one's heart neatly.
Being asked what is unfitting, I don't know what it is.
But my heart knows somehow.
I feel irresistible desire to know what a mystery a human is.
As to this mystery, clarifying, knowing how to live, knowing how to talk with people, demonstrating and teaching this is the Buddha from my human eyes, I feel it's really impossible to become Buddha.
But this I, regarding what the Buddha does, vows to practice, to aspire, to be resolute, and tells myself, yes, I will just practice right here now and achieve continuity endlessly, forever.
This is living in vow.
This is one's peaceful life found.
Yeah.
Herein is one's peaceful life found.
Yes, just practice right here now.
That's it.*
I don't know if you know, but in Zen, the names we give are basically two names.
Like my name is Shudo Kanho, protector of the way, complete release.
The first name is often a little bit of an attaboy, like you're doing great.
That was Tony, completely rooted.
He knew his life; he really was present.
He was really there for a lot of it, and there was nothing left out.
His second name that I chose for him was peaceful way.
Now, that was also an attaboy.
Usually it's more like an encouragement, like, "Could you please work on this a little bit more?"
Which is why I'm grabby by nature; that's why my name is complete release.
Because I had a lot of work to do with letting go of things and stories and patterns and all these.
So Tony was absolutely peaceful with where he was and what was going to happen pretty soon.
His wife, Rosemary, was also so amazing.
I mean, he was very much impacted physically by his disease, but there was not any reluctance or hesitation or anything on Rosemary's side.
She just fully was there, and it was wonderful to watch.
I guess you all know what I'm going to say next.
Tony passed away yesterday.
Rosemary was the one who sent me the sad email, but she also said how much Chukai and practicing with and around the precepts had meant for Tony.
So, dear Tony, benefactor of the Sangha, thank you for sharing your heart, your big heart with us for a while.
All your life was rooted in service to under-resourced populations, and you will be missed.
Tony did truly let the myriad things come forth and experience themselves.
He was even curious about his health in an almost neutral way, and in spite of long, severe sickness, he delighted in that experience.
Continuing with Genjokoan, to carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion.
That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.
Those who have great realization of delusion are Buddhas.
Those who are greatly deluded about realization are sentient beings.
Further, there are those who continue realizing beyond realization, who are in delusion throughout delusion.
When Buddhas are truly Buddhas, they do not necessarily notice that they are Buddhas.
However, they are actualized Buddhas who go on actualizing Buddhas.
So I thought we might do something a little bit different again this time.
And there is a koan in the Blue Cliff Record, koan number 55, also known as Dao Wu's condolence call.
I'll read it to you.
*Dao Wu and his disciple Jin Yuan went to a house to make a condolence call.
This is happening in eighth century China.
So at that time, monks and priests didn't do funeral services like they're doing nowadays.
They just visit the family to acknowledge the deceased.
But while they're there, the monk Jin Yuan hits the coffin and says, "Dao Wu said, I won't say your life, and I won't say dead."
Jin Yuan said, "Why won't you say?"
Dao Wu said, "I won't say, I won't say."
I really wonder what was the family thinking about all that.*
So halfway back to the monastery, Jin Yuan said, "Tell me right away, teacher, life or dead.
If you don't tell me, I will hit you."
Dao Wu said, "You may hit me, but I won't say."
So, Jin Yuan, true to his word, it is teacher.
Also got kicked out of the monastery, and he became a wandering monk.
Well, in time, Dao Wu died.
And Jin Yuan went to study with Master Qishuang.
He told his new teacher about this exchange with Dao Wu and asked about his point of view.
Qishuang said, "I won't say life, and I won't say dead."
Jin Yuan said, "Why won't you say?"
Qishuang just said, "I won't say, I won't say."
And at these words, Jin Yuan had an insight.
Later, Jin Yuan, carrying a hoe, went up and down in the lecture hall as if he were searching for something.
Qishuang said, "What are you doing?"
Jin Yuan said, "I am searching for the spiritual remains of our dead teacher."
Qishuang said, "Limitless expanse of mighty roaring waves.
Foaming waves wash the sky.
What relic of the deceased teacher do you seek?"
I'm going to stop the recording now so we can have some discussion time around this.
